structured_output.title: A base of "/admin" no longer claims "/admin-dashboard"
structured_output.premise: A Nuxt app set `baseURL: '/admin/'` and had a page at `/admin-dashboard` (nuxt/nuxt#33924). `withoutBase` only checked `startsWith`, so it cut "/admin" off the page path and routed to "/-dashboard". `withBase` had the same flaw the other way round: it decided "/admin-dashboard" already had the "/admin" base and returned it without adding the prefix.
structured_output.verdict: Both functions now count the base as present only when the next character is "/", "?" or the end of the string. Four tests that failed before now pass, and the other 28 still pass. Risk: "#" is not treated as a boundary, so "/admin#top" with base "/admin" now gets different results in both functions, and no test covers that. Callers that depended on the old loose prefix matching will also see different output.

chapters.title: Removing the base no longer cuts "/admin" out of "/admin-dashboard"
chapters.before: withoutBase("/admin-dashboard", "/admin/" or "/admin") matched "/admin" as a prefix and returned "/-dashboard".
chapters.after: The character after "/admin" is "-", so withoutBase returns "/admin-dashboard" unchanged. "/admin/dashboard" still becomes "/dashboard".
facts: The new guard (lines 326-330) returns the input unchanged when nextChar exists and is not "/" or "?".
Before the change, both failing tests raised AssertionError "expected '/-dashboard' to be '/admin-dashboard'".
"/admin/admin-dashboard" with base "/admin/" still returns "/admin-dashboard" (line 226): only the first segment is compared.
"#" is not in the allowed set, so "/admin#x" with base "/admin" now comes back unchanged. Before, it became "/#x". No test covers this; the claim rests on the code alone.

open_questions.question: Does the stricter check still strip the base when a query string follows it directly, as in "/api?test", or when the input is exactly the base?

chapters.title: Adding the base now prefixes "/admin-dashboard" instead of skipping it
chapters.before: withBase("/admin-dashboard", "/admin/" or "/admin") saw the "/admin" prefix and returned "/admin-dashboard" with no base added.
chapters.after: nextChar is "-", so the code falls through to joinURL("/admin", "/admin-dashboard"), which returns "/admin/admin-dashboard".
facts: The joinURL → withTrailingSlash calls on lines 77-82 and 99-104 happen only on the head side.
Before the change, both tests raised AssertionError "expected '/admin-dashboard' to be '/admin/admin-dashboard'".
"/admin/admin-dashboard" and "/admin/dashboard" with base "/admin/" are still returned unchanged, because nextChar is "/".
Same "#" gap here: withBase("/admin#x", "/admin") now returns "/admin/admin#x". Before, it returned "/admin#x". This is untested and rests on the code alone.

open_questions.question: Do the existing cases where the input already carries the base ("/base", "/base/", "/base/a") or is an absolute URL still come back untouched?

chapters.title: Genuine base matches, including a query right after the base, are still removed
chapters.before: "/api?test" with base "/api" became "/?test", "/base/a" became "/a", and "/base" with base "/base/" became "/".
chapters.after: Same results: nextChar is "?", "/" or undefined, so the guard lets each input through to the existing slice.
facts: The "?" boundary is covered only by the "/api?test"-"/api" case (line 196).
The end-of-string boundary is covered by "/base"-"/base/" and "/base/a"-"/base/a/", which both return "/".
A root base "/" exits early through isEmptyURL before the new check runs (lines 118, 181, 188, 209).

answers.answer: Yes. "/api?test" with base "/api" still becomes "/?test" because nextChar "?" is allowed. When the input is exactly the base, nextChar is undefined and the result is still "/".

chapters.title: Inputs that already carry the base are still left alone
chapters.before: "/base", "/base/" and "/base/a" with base "/base" or "/base/" came back unchanged, and "/bar" became "/foo/bar".
chapters.after: Identical results: nextChar is undefined or "/", so the input is returned. Protocol URLs and root bases still exit early.
facts: None of the withBase tests here exercise a "?" right after the base, so that branch of the new condition is untested for withBase.
"https://test.com" returns early through hasProtocol or isEmptyURL and never reaches the new check.

answers.answer: Yes. All ten original withBase tests return the same values on both sides. Inputs at a real boundary (nextChar undefined or "/") are returned as they are, and absolute URLs exit before the check.
